prompt_text:
The figure summarizes how activating p53 can make tumors more visible to the immune system and improve response to anti-PD1 therapy. In the basal state, p53 is restrained by MDM2/MDMX, while chromatin-modifying enzymes such as LSD1, SETDB1, SUV39H1, and DNMT1 keep repetitive transposable elements (RTEs) in closed, silenced chromatin through repressive histone and DNA methylation marks.

When p53 is activated, apparently by blocking MDM2/MDMX, this repression is relieved. p53 accumulates on chromatin, RTEs become more open, and their transcripts generate viral-like nucleic acid signals. The diagram shows both cytosolic DNA and double-stranded RNA sensing pathways being engaged, including cGAS-STING, TLR3, and MDA5, which then trigger IRF3 and JAK-STAT signaling and increase interferon production. At the same time, antigen presentation appears to rise, including MHC class II, making the tumor more immunogenic.

The right side links these tumor-cell changes to the immune microenvironment: anti-PD1 acts on PD1-positive CD8+ T cells, and together with p53 activation it boosts T-cell function, cytotoxic molecules such as granzyme and perforin, and overall antitumor activity. The main message is a synergy between p53 reactivation and checkpoint blockade that suppresses tumor growth.
